text: Everything so far has been setup. This lesson writes the actual query that answers the question the VP of Support asked back in lesson one: how many tickets came in each day this month, broken down by priority.

Here's the full query. It selects the ticket's created-at timestamp, truncated to a plain calendar day, the priority column, and a count — filtered down to this month, grouped by day and priority, ordered the same way. Three things are doing real work here. The WHERE clause keeps only this month's rows, before anything gets grouped. DATE_TRUNC collapses each ticket's exact timestamp down to its calendar day. And GROUP BY with COUNT, together, produce exactly the grain this project decided on back in lesson one — one row per day, per priority.

It's tempting to write GROUP BY first and filter afterward with HAVING, but that's the wrong tool here. HAVING filters groups, after they're already formed. WHERE filters raw rows, before any grouping happens — which means Snowflake never even has to touch last month's rows at all. Correct, and cheaper.

Before anyone presents this number, it's worth a quick sanity check. Rolling the daily counts back up into one total per priority, across the whole month, is a fast way to catch an obviously wrong query — say, a count that's ten times too high — before it ever reaches the VP.

That's the whole summary query: filtered to this month, grouped to the right grain, with a quick way to check its own math. It's a handful of lines of SQL, and it's the actual deliverable this entire project exists to produce.
The query works, but right now anyone with access to Snowflake could run it. Next lesson, basic RBAC: one read-only role, so the right person can see this summary — and nothing beyond it.
